title.en: Can Taiwan Really Reach Its Renewable Energy Target?

A2.text: Look at the new wind turbines on our west coast. See the solar panels on school roofs. Is Taiwan really turning green fast, or is that just talk?

B1.text: You can see wind turbines along our western beaches, and solar panels on our classroom roofs. But has Taiwan actually become green, or does it only talk about it?

B2.text: While wind turbines now line our beaches and solar panels blanket rooftops, one question still lingers unresolved. Is Taiwan really greening as quickly as it claims, or only appearing to?

title.en: SDG 7: A Target, Not Just a Feeling

A2.text: SDG 7 means clean, safe, modern energy for everyone. This talk is not about climate change. It is about our energy targets, and whether we hit them.

B1.text: SDG 7 promises affordable, reliable energy for everyone, though today we will not discuss climate change, because that belongs elsewhere. This talk instead is about our targets and our reality.

B2.text: SDG 7 demands affordable, reliable and sustainable energy for everyone, though this talk will not dwell on climate change itself. It instead interrogates the gap between the targets Taiwan has set and what has actually been delivered.

A2.text: In 2017, Taiwan made a new law for 2025. Renewables should reach 20 percent. Coal should be 30 percent, and gas 50 percent. Today we test that 20 percent number.

B1.text: In 2017, Taiwan's lawmakers locked in a 20-30-50 formula for 2025. Renewables would supply 20 percent of the grid, coal 30 percent, and gas the remaining 50 percent.

B2.text: In 2017, Taiwan legislated the 20-30-50 generation mix for 2025, mandating 20 percent renewables alongside coal and gas. It is precisely this 20 percent figure that will be tested today.

stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...

A2.text: Look at Taiwan's real numbers from 2024. Clean energy reached only 11.6 percent. The target was 20 percent. Coal and gas still make over 80 percent of our power.

B1.text: The real numbers from 2024 tell a different story. Renewables have only reached 11.6 percent, which falls far short of the 20 percent goal, while gas and coal still dominate the grid.

B2.text: The 2024 figures tell a far less flattering story. Renewables, reaching only 11.6 percent, fell well short of the 20 percent mandate, while fossil fuels still supplied over 80 percent of the country's electricity.

A2.text: Our solar goal was 20 gigawatts by 2025. We only built about 15. The work is slow. Land fights and strict rules cause long delays for new panels.

B1.text: The solar target was 20 gigawatts by 2025, yet only about 15 have been installed so far. Tighter rules and land disputes have slowed the permitting process across the island.

B2.text: Although the official 2025 solar target stood at 20 gigawatts, barely 15 have so far been installed. That gap is largely explained by land-use conflicts and very strict permitting rules.

A2.text: We wanted 5.7 gigawatts by 2025. We only reached 4.9. New turbines take too long to build, because costs are high and parts are hard to get.

B1.text: Offshore wind aimed for 5.7 gigawatts, but Taiwan has only reached about 4.9. Rising costs and global supply problems have made recent auctions weaker than planners had hoped.

B2.text: Offshore wind is missing its target too, capping out at roughly 4.9 of a planned 5.7 gigawatts. This shortfall stems primarily from global supply chains and financing costs that have squeezed recent auctions harder than expected.

title.en: Third in the World, Behind Our Own Bar
title.zh: 世界第三，落後自己的目標

A2.text: We missed our own goal, but we still did well. Taiwan added more new wind power than most countries in 2025. We now rank third in the whole world.

B1.text: Even though Taiwan missed its own target, the record still looks strong worldwide. Taiwan has ranked third globally for new offshore wind added in 2025, ahead of most nations.

B2.text: Despite missing its own target, Taiwan's progress reads as significant worldwide. Ranked third for new offshore wind added in 2025, the country now has more capacity than most developed economies.

title.en: Panels on Roofs, Ponds and Fields
title.zh: 屋頂、魚塭與廠房上的光電板

A2.text: You can see the difference when you travel. Solar panels now sit on school roofs and over fish ponds. Wind power grew fast too. It is much bigger than before.

B1.text: The landscape has genuinely changed around us. Solar panels have spread across fish ponds, school roofs and factory buildings, while wind generation has grown by 66 percent in one year.

B2.text: Solar installations built on fish ponds, school roofs and factory buildings have visibly reshaped the landscape. Wind generation, meanwhile, has climbed 66 percent in a single year, far faster than planners expected.

title.en: Moving the Deadline, Not the Target

A2.text: The government did not cancel the target. They just moved the deadline to November 2026. This new date sounds far away, but we still need much more power.

B1.text: The government has not cancelled its 20 percent goal. Instead, it has pushed the deadline to November 2026, a date that still demands far more power than Taiwan produces right now.

B2.text: Rather than abandoning the shortfall quietly, the government has postponed the 20 percent deadline to November 2026. Meeting even this revised target, however, will demand a construction pace far above current trends.

A2.text: How can we fix this? Instead of making solar firms wait for years, Taiwan must change the rules. Leaders should make land permits faster for everyone.

B1.text: Solving the solar delay means reforming the land rules first. Instead of leaving approvals to scattered local offices, the central government could step in so permits move much faster.

B2.text: Fixing the solar shortfall needs real permitting reform. Instead of leaving land-use approvals to scattered local offices, one central authority should handle them, so installations can move ahead without delay.

A2.text: For wind power, we must bring investors back. Instead of running small auctions, Taiwan should offer bigger, safer deals. This could help pay for rising costs.

B1.text: Winning back investor trust matters just as much for wind power. Instead of holding small, weak auctions, Taiwan should offer bigger contracts that can actually cover today's higher turbine costs.

B2.text: Investor confidence in offshore wind must also be restored. Instead of running weak auctions, Taiwan should guarantee larger rounds, which could offset some of the inflation squeezing global supply chains.

title.en: Betting on Hydrogen and Geothermal Too

A2.text: We can also try new energy, like hydrogen and heat from the earth. Instead of only using wind and sun, we should test these too. New tech may take longer.

B1.text: The 2050 plan also counts on hydrogen and geothermal power. Instead of relying only on solar and wind, Taiwan should diversify, though newer options will need more time to mature.

B2.text: The 2050 pathway also includes hydrogen and geothermal power. Instead of relying only on proven renewables, Taiwan should diversify, although this trades the readiness of wind and solar for technology that remains unproven.

A2.text: Our chip factories use huge amounts of power. Global buyers want green power for their chips. Without it, they may look elsewhere. That is a real risk for Taiwan.

B1.text: Our chip plants use huge amounts of power every single day. If verified green power is not delivered soon, global clients that demand it could simply take their business elsewhere.

B2.text: Taiwan's chip industry uses vast amounts of electricity. If clean power is not delivered quickly enough, global clients may look elsewhere, turning an environmental shortfall into a genuine competitive risk.

A2.text: We must meet the new 2026 date. If we miss it again, investors may lose trust. Less trust means higher costs, and that stops more new projects.

B1.text: The pressure is now on that new 2026 date. If this delayed goal slips again, investor trust will weaken further, and weaker trust is exactly what caused the last shortfall.

B2.text: The new November 2026 date is therefore quite critical for everyone involved. If this target is missed once again, investor confidence will drop even further, causing the same problem that produced the original shortfall in the first place.

title.en: Who Hosts the Turbines, Who Gets the Power
title.zh: 誰承擔風機，誰享用電力

A2.text: This problem needs more than money to fix. If we build wind farms fast, local towns feel the change first. People near the turbines do not always get the power.

B1.text: Restoring that trust is not only about money, though money matters too. If wind farms are built too quickly, local communities could feel the disruption first, without gaining much power.

B2.text: Restoring credibility, however, extends beyond financial metrics alone. Should deployment be pushed forward too fast, host communities will bear the physical impact, even though they rarely benefit from the power generated.

title.en: The Real Test: Delivery, Not Announcement
title.zh: 真正的考驗：兌現而非宣布

A2.text: So this problem is not only about money. If we only chase one number, we lose people's trust. The real test is hitting the goal, and keeping that trust too.

B1.text: These economic and local pressures are all closely connected. If we ignore the communities that host this equipment, public support will fade fast, so the real test is keeping trust.

B2.text: These economic and equity concerns are inextricably linked to one another. Only when community voices are genuinely respected will public support remain intact, and hitting a target is never the same as sustaining people's trust.

title.en: Progress and the Gap, Side by Side

A2.text: To wrap up, we made real progress. We built new turbines and reached a top world ranking. But our real numbers are still far from our own legal target.

B1.text: To wrap up, real progress clearly exists across Taiwan today. We have built turbines, spread solar panels, and earned a top-five global ranking, yet our reality sits behind our legal targets.

B2.text: To wrap up, although real progress is evident, from growing turbines to a top-five global ranking, a real gap remains. Our generation reality still sits well behind the statutory targets we ourselves set.

title.zh: 由你們這代人補上缺口

A2.text: This matters to you right now. You are Taiwan's future engineers. You will build the grids and the batteries. Your work can finally close this big energy gap.

B1.text: This gap matters to everyone sitting in this room. You are the students who will become the engineers designing the grid connections and storage systems that finally close this divide.

B2.text: This shortfall carries particular weight for a STEM audience. It is you who will engineer the solutions, designing the grid infrastructure and storage systems required to finally close this gap.

title.zh: 該問「做到了嗎」，別只問「說了嗎」

A2.text: Let's look at the facts closely. Do not just ask what leaders promised. Ask what they actually built. Join local talks about where new solar farms should go.

B1.text: Let's study the data much more critically from now on. Stop asking only what was announced, and start asking what has actually been delivered, then join the debates that shape it.

B2.text: Let's commit to reading the data more critically from now on. We must look beyond announced ambitions and demand delivered results, then take part in the local debates where these decisions are actually made.

title.en: Move the Date, Not the Destination
title.zh: 日期可以延，目的地不能變

A2.text: Remember one last thing before we go. The target date may move again someday. But our green destination must never, ever change. Let's finish this whole job together.

B1.text: Let's carry just one thought forward from today. Governments can always push a deadline back, but our destination should never move, so let's make sure Taiwan actually arrives there.

B2.text: Let's close with a guiding principle for the years ahead. The government may shift its deadlines once again, although our ultimate destination must remain fixed, because real change only counts once delivered.
